$comment: Findings check-org-sentinel-reads.mjs knows about and does not fail on.
A waiver matches ONE site, ONE capability, and ONE exact set of offending
tables. Anything else is a new finding: a table the handler did not narrow
before, a different capability, a moved file. The table set is in the match
identity on purpose — without it a waiver would keep matching after the
handler grew a second narrowed table, suppressing a new defect while still
It RATCHETS DOWN: an entry matching no finding is itself an error, so an
entry cannot outlive the defect it waives, and a defect that changes shape
reports twice — once as a new finding, once as a stale waiver.
Two kinds. `waived` is a real defect whose fix belongs to another change;
`acknowledged` is not a defect at all — something this check reports that a
more precise analysis would not, with `needs` naming which analysis. An
acknowledged entry without `needs` is rejected, so the category cannot
become a place to put anything inconvenient.
Add a waiver only for a live instance whose fix belongs to a different
change, and name that change in `fixedBy` so the entry has an owner and an
end. Never add either kind to make your own diff pass.

acknowledged.needs: path sensitivity, then interprocedural constant propagation
acknowledged.reason: Not a defect. listMembersHandler branches on `input.scope`: the org branch reads org.org_users and org.invitations, both org_only and correct under the sentinel; the workspace branch reads workspace.workspace_users. This call site passes `input: { scope: "org" }`, so the workspace branch never runs. The check pools the tables of every withTenantDb region in a handler, because knowing which branch a sentinel-scoped call takes means evaluating a condition on an input supplied in another file. This entry is evidence for ADR-074's assessment that the static approach does not converge: it appeared the moment the table resolver closed the aliasing gap.
